role: Foremost Quran Reciter among the Companions
Personal Scribe of the Prophet ﷺ
One of the Four Quran Compilers
summary: Ubay ibn Ka'b (RA) was the foremost Quran reciter among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and one of his personal scribes. He memorized the Quran directly from the Prophet ﷺ and was praised by name as the best reciter of the Sahaba. His recitation formed one of the authoritative chains through which the Quran was transmitted.
biography:
Ubay ibn Ka'b al-Ansari al-Khazraji was born in Madinah into the Banu al-Najjar clan of the Khazraj tribe. He was among the earliest converts from the Ansar (Helpers of Madinah), accepting Islam before the Hijrah of the Prophet ﷺ. Even before the advent of Islam, Ubay was literate — a rare distinction in Arabia at that time — and this skill made him invaluable to the early Muslim community.

The Prophet ﷺ appointed Ubay as one of his personal scribes, tasked with recording Quranic revelations. Ibn Sa'd records in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra that Ubay was among the most skilled of the scribes, alongside Zayd ibn Thabit. His deep familiarity with the Quran came not only from transcription but from repeated direct recitation with the Prophet ﷺ himself.

The Prophet ﷺ praised Ubay's recitation explicitly and frequently. In the hadith recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'The best reciter of my ummah is Ubay ibn Ka'b.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab Fada'il al-Quran). This statement established him as the authoritative reference for Quranic recitation during and after the Prophet's lifetime.

One of the most remarkable distinctions of Ubay ibn Ka'b was the honor of completing a full recitation (khatm) of the Quran directly with the Prophet ﷺ in the final Ramadan before the Prophet's death. Ibn Kathir records in al-Bidayah wal-Nihayah that the Prophet ﷺ reviewed the Quran twice with Jibril (AS) in that last year, and Ubay was the Companion chosen to recite on behalf of the ummah in this blessed review. This event is considered evidence of Ubay's singular standing among all the huffadh (memorizers).

The Prophet ﷺ also instructed other Companions to learn the Quran specifically from Ubay. In a hadith narrated by Anas ibn Malik and recorded by al-Bukhari: 'Collect the Quran from four: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Salim, Mu'adh, and Ubay ibn Ka'b.' This directive placed Ubay among the four primary Quranic authorities — a status that structured the transmission of Quranic knowledge to subsequent generations.

Beyond recitation, Ubay was known as a man of deep knowledge and piety. He narrated a large number of hadith and is recorded as having transmitted approximately 164 narrations in the major collections. He was known to be emotionally moved during worship, weeping in salah, and spending long hours in night prayer.

His legal opinions (fatwas) were sought during the caliphates of Abu Bakr and Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA). Umar held him in great respect and would frequently defer to Ubay on matters pertaining to the Quran. According to al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala', Umar once said during a sermon: 'Ubay is the master of the Muslims' (sayyid al-muslimin) in Quranic matters.

During the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, when the tarawih prayers in Ramadan were organized as a congregation led by a single imam, Umar appointed Ubay ibn Ka'b to lead the prayer for the men, underscoring his unsurpassed standing as a reciter. This decision by Umar is recorded by Ibn Sa'd and al-Bayhaqi.

Ubay ibn Ka'b died in Madinah during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan, around 30 AH (650 CE), though some scholars record his death as early as 19 AH or as late as 32 AH. Al-Dhahabi notes the disagreement in dates but places the weight of evidence closer to 30 AH. He left behind a legacy as the foundational link in the chain of Quranic recitation, and every Muslim who recites the Quran today owes a measure of that preservation to Ubay ibn Ka'b.
